content: During the Great Plague of 1665, the region of Derby in England was severely affected by the bubonic plague, resulting in a significant number of deaths. Certain areas in Derby still bear names that reflect the events of that year. For instance, Blagreaves Lane was originally called Black Graves, and Dead Man's Lane is self-explanatory in its grim reference to the plague's toll. Some historians have suggested that bodies were buried in an upright position at St. Peter's Church in Derby during this time. However, this claim has been thoroughly debunked by experts and is now considered a myth. Trade during the epidemic was conducted at a Market Stone located on Ashbourne Road, which leads into the town center. The outbreak caused trade to nearly come to a halt, leaving the population at risk of starvation in addition to the devastating effects of the plague itself. The Market Stone served as a critical point for transactions during this period of crisis. Market stones varied in design, and one notable example in Derby was situated at Friar Gate, previously known as Nuns Green, on the northern road into the town. This particular stone was a medieval headless cross, also referred to as the Vinegar Stone. It earned this name because coins were placed in a trough filled with vinegar at the top of the stone. This practice was based on the belief that vinegar could disinfect the money and prevent the transmission of the plague.
